case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim can proceed when probable cause existed for the arrest, based on objective evidence that similarly situated people not engaged in protected speech are typically not arrested (the Nieves exception), and what a plaintiff must plead/prove to satisfy that exception.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (retaliation for protected speech/petitioning) enforced through 42 U.S.C. § 1983; interacting doctrinally with the probable-cause rule for retaliatory arrest announced in Nieves v. Bartlett.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Gonzalez argues that local officials orchestrated her arrest in retaliation for her political speech and participation in city governance, and that the Fifth Circuit applied an overly rigid version of Nieves’s “objective evidence” exception by effectively demanding near-identical comparator arrests and discounting contextual objective proof (including the unusual use of a seldom-enforced statute and the particular sequence of events) showing that similarly situated people who did not engage in the same protected activity are ordinarily not arrested. She contends the exception should be practically available where objective indicia show retaliatory enforcement, even if probable cause technically existed.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that because there was probable cause to arrest Gonzalez, Nieves generally bars her retaliatory-arrest claim and she cannot fit within Nieves’s narrow exception absent clear, objective comparator evidence demonstrating that others engaged in the same conduct (but not the same speech) are not arrested. They maintain the Fifth Circuit correctly required stringent objective proof to avoid turning routine arrests supported by probable cause into retaliation litigation based on disputed motive, and that easing the standard would chill law enforcement and burden local governments with broad discovery into officials’ subjective intent.
key_precedents: Mt. Healthy City School District Board of Education v. Doyle (1977)
Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach (2018)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest argument is that a near-identical comparator requirement could make Nieves’s “objective evidence” qualification practically unavailable in discretionary-arrest contexts; I take that concern seriously. But Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Jackson’s proposed acceptance of policies or statistics, even if labeled “objective,” predictably invites denominator disputes and context-heavy line-drawing that dilutes Nieves’s probable-cause screen and recreates the motive-centered discovery burdens Hartman and Reichle sought to prevent. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Lozman does not move me because Lozman’s municipal-policy posture was expressly exceptional and did not purport to revise the ordinary arrest/probable-cause framework that governs here. On minimalist, administrability grounds, I would affirm a comparator-tethered understanding of “objective evidence,” while leaving a narrow opening for truly concrete comparator substitutes that function with comparable specificity.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that an overly rigid, near-identical-comparator demand could make Nieves’s “objective evidence” qualification difficult to satisfy in discretionary, rarely enforced contexts, but that policy concern cannot justify converting Nieves’s probable-cause rule into a generalized patterns-and-statistics regime that reintroduces the intent-focused litigation Hartman and Reichle sought to prevent. Justice Gorsuch’s proposal to treat enforcement patterns as “objective evidence,” even with limiting language, predictably shifts the inquiry to denominator disputes and discretionary line-drawing, functionally downgrading probable cause from a categorical screen to one factor in a totality test. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Lozman does not move me because Lozman involved a distinct municipal-policy posture and expressly did not unsettle the ordinary arrest/probable-cause framework; it therefore cannot expand Nieves beyond its comparative, similarly situated logic. On a textualist/originalist approach to this Court’s existing § 1983 causation screens, I would adhere to a narrow, comparator-tethered exception and affirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that a near-identical-comparator requirement could make Nieves’s “objective evidence” qualification difficult to use for rarely enforced, discretionary offenses, but that practical concern cannot justify transforming a narrow carveout into an open-ended enforcement-pattern and statistics inquiry that revives motive-centered litigation. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Nieves framed the exception in comparative, administrable terms—objective proof that similarly situated non-speakers are typically not arrested—which requires a concrete, materially similar comparator (or a true substitute that is comparably determinate), not contested debates over denominators and local discretion. Hartman and Reichle reinforce why probable cause must remain a categorical screen in this context; diluting it into just one factor, as Justice Gorsuch’s approach risks doing, undermines the rule’s function and invites intrusive discovery into officers’ motives. Lozman, invoked by Justice Sotomayor, was a distinct municipal-policy case and does not warrant expanding ordinary arrest-retaliation claims beyond Nieves’s narrow, comparator-tethered exception when probable cause exists.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s strongest point is administrability: if “objective evidence” devolves into open-ended patterns-and-statistics disputes, Nieves’s probable-cause screen could be swallowed by motive-driven discovery. But Justice Kagan is right that the Fifth Circuit’s near-identical-comparator demand functionally nullifies Nieves’s expressly preserved safety valve in the very discretionary, rarely enforced offenses where retaliation is most plausible and “exact twins” rarely exist. Hartman and Reichle support screening mechanisms, yet they do not authorize rewriting Nieves’s carveout into a dead letter; the better reading—consistent with Justice Barrett’s own limiting principle—is to allow comparator-analog objective evidence (policy, customary non-enforcement, or reliable, tightly tethered statistics) that shows materially similar non-speakers are typically not arrested. Lozman, while factually distinct, reinforces my pragmatic concern that rigid categorical rules should not foreclose plausible retaliation claims where objective indicia of targeting exist.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point—administrability and avoiding denominator fights that invite motive discovery—matters, but it cannot justify a reading of Nieves that effectively nullifies its own “objective evidence” clause by insisting on a near-identical twin comparator in discretionary-arrest settings. Justice Barrett is right to demand that any patterns evidence do real comparative work; my answer is to treat policies, customary non-enforcement, or reliable statistics as admissible only when tightly tethered to materially similar conduct and offered as a gatekeeping substitute for a one-to-one comparator, not as a backdoor motive probe. Hartman and Reichle (as Justice Thomas emphasizes) support probable cause as a causation screen, but they do not address Nieves’s explicit carveout, so textual coherence requires giving that exception operative effect rather than shrinking it to vanishing point. Lozman does not expand the ordinary framework, but it reinforces that we should not adopt categorical rules so rigid that they foreclose retaliation claims even when objective indicia of aberrational enforcement exist.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Alito press the best administrability point: if “objective evidence” devolves into free-form disputes about enforcement discretion and statistical denominators, we risk erasing Nieves’s probable-cause screen and inviting motive discovery. But Justice Barrett’s limiting principle answers that concern without rewriting Nieves’s qualification out of existence: pattern or policy evidence counts only insofar as it functions as a genuine comparator substitute—tethered to materially similar conduct and demonstrating that non-speakers are ordinarily not arrested. Justice Thomas is right that Hartman and Reichle require a causation screen, yet Nieves itself carved out a narrow, objective exception, and a near-identical-comparator requirement effectively nullifies that text in the very discretionary-offense setting Nieves identified. Lozman does not expand the ordinary framework, but it underscores that we should not adopt categorical rules that foreclose retaliation claims where objective indicia of targeting can be shown without probing intent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest opposing point: a near-identical-twin comparator can render Nieves’s “objective evidence” qualification difficult to satisfy for rarely enforced, discretionary offenses. But Nieves characterized that carveout as a “narrow qualification,” and—consistent with Hartman and Reichle’s administrable causation screens—I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that opening the door to generalized “patterns” or statistics will predictably devolve into denominator disputes and discretionary line-drawing that functionally reintroduce motive-centric litigation despite probable cause. I can accept, as Justice Barrett suggests, only those non-individualized proofs that operate as a genuine comparator substitute—tightly tethered to materially similar conduct and showing ordinary non-arrest—yet on this record the petitioner’s theory is too elastic and risks converting probable cause from a threshold bar into a factor. Lozman, invoked by Justice Sotomayor, does not move me because it involved an atypical municipal-policy posture and expressly did not unsettle the ordinary arrest/probable-cause framework that governs here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch are right that a near-identical “twin” comparator is not always available, and Nieves’s “typically” language must have some operative work to do. But that does not justify converting the exception into a generalized “patterns and statistics” inquiry untethered to materially similar conduct, which (as the Chief Justice notes) predictably devolves into denominator disputes and resurrects the motive-focused litigation Hartman and Reichle sought to screen out. I can accept Justice Gorsuch’s idea only insofar as enforcement-pattern evidence functions as a genuine comparator substitute—concrete proof that non-speakers engaging in materially similar conduct are ordinarily not arrested—yet the Fifth Circuit’s comparator-tethered approach remains the best administrable proxy for that requirement. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Lozman does not move me because it arose from an atypical municipal-policy theory and expressly did not unsettle the ordinary-arrest/probable-cause framework that governs here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s administrability concern is the strongest point for the Respondent, and I share the view (echoed by Justice Barrett) that “objective evidence” cannot become an amorphous, denominator-driven patterns inquiry that invites intent discovery through the back door. But the Fifth Circuit’s near-identical-comparator gloss effectively nullifies Nieves’s expressly preserved safety valve in the very discretionary, rarely enforced contexts Nieves identified—where one-to-one comparators predictably do not exist—thereby undermining procedural fairness and leaving plausible retaliation claims without any realistic path past the threshold. Hartman and Reichle support a causation screen, not a rewriting of the carveout into a dead letter; a pragmatic rule can require tight, offense-and-circumstances tethering (policy, customary non-arrest practice, or reliable statistics) as a comparator substitute without authorizing motive probing at the pleading stage. Lozman, while atypical, reinforces that categorical barriers should not foreclose claims when objective indicia of targeting exist, and that principle counsels giving Nieves’s exception operative effect rather than collapsing it into an “exact twin” requirement.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Nieves v. Bartlett (2019), the existence of probable cause generally bars a § 1983 First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim, with only a narrow exception requiring objective evidence that similarly situated individuals not engaged in protected speech are typically not arrested. Preserving that objective, administrable limit protects institutional legitimacy by avoiding motive-based litigation over routine arrests and aligns with Hartman v. Moore (2006) and Reichle v. Howards (2012), which emphasize causation and the screening function of probable-cause requirements in retaliation contexts. Given the materials suggesting this arrest involved a more serious, non-petty offense and was not a paradigmatic “rarely-arrested” minor infraction, I would not expand Nieves’s exception beyond its narrow terms, and would affirm the Fifth Circuit’s stringent objective-evidence requirement. Federalism and respect for local law-enforcement discretion counsel in favor of a narrow ruling that leaves broader adjustments to legislatures or future cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First Amendment’s text does not create a freestanding damages action for arrests supported by probable cause, and in § 1983 we have required objective, administrable limits to avoid turning routine criminal enforcement into litigation over officials’ subjective motives. Nieves v. Bartlett held that probable cause “should generally defeat” a retaliatory-arrest claim, recognizing only a “narrow qualification” where officers ordinarily decline to arrest for the offense and the plaintiff presents objective comparative evidence that similarly situated persons not engaged in protected speech were not arrested. Consistent with Hartman v. Moore’s causation/probable-cause rule and Reichle v. Howards’ emphasis on clear constraints in this area, the Fifth Circuit’s insistence on a stringent, objective showing properly cabins the exception and respects the States’ primary authority over criminal law enforcement. Because petitioner’s proposed broader standard would effectively revive motive-based liability despite probable cause, I would affirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett established a general rule that the existence of probable cause defeats a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim, with only a narrow exception requiring “objective evidence” that similarly situated individuals not engaged in protected speech are typically not arrested. Expanding that exception beyond clear comparator/non-enforcement proof would reintroduce the very motive-driven litigation Nieves sought to avoid, imposing substantial practical burdens on law enforcement and local governments through intrusive discovery into subjective intent. This approach is consistent with Hartman v. Moore’s insistence on a probable-cause screen in retaliation contexts and with Reichle v. Howards’ warning against exposing officers to liability when probable cause exists. Because Gonzalez has not shown the kind of concrete, objective comparator evidence Nieves demands, § 1983 liability under the First Amendment should not lie here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett makes probable cause a general bar to § 1983 retaliatory-arrest claims, but it also preserves an “objective evidence” pathway where the challenged enforcement is atypical and thus more plausibly retaliatory, especially for offenses that are rarely enforced through arrest. The Fifth Circuit’s near-identical-comparator demand unduly narrows that exception and risks insulating selective, speech-targeted enforcement from any remedy, contrary to the First Amendment’s core prohibition on retaliation for protected participation in civic life and petitioning. Consistent with Mt. Healthy’s but-for causation framework and Lozman’s recognition that retaliation claims cannot be foreclosed by rigid rules when objective indicia support animus, a plaintiff should be permitted to plead and prove the Nieves exception through practical, objective proof of non-enforcement patterns (e.g., policy, statistics, or customary practice), not solely one-to-one comparator arrests. This approach preserves Nieves’s administrability while ensuring meaningful access to justice for speakers plausibly singled out by government officials despite technical probable cause.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett makes probable cause a general bar to First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claims, but it also recognizes a narrow, administrable “objective evidence” pathway where arrest is atypical and discretionary and similarly situated non-speakers are generally not arrested. The Fifth Circuit’s near-identical-comparator demand risks collapsing that exception into a nullity, contrary to Nieves’s own rationale and to Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach’s recognition that retaliatory enforcement can sometimes be shown without turning every case into a motive inquiry. To preserve statutory coherence under § 1983 and workable line-drawing, a plaintiff should be allowed to satisfy the Nieves exception with objective, context-sensitive proof (including reliable enforcement patterns for the charged offense) demonstrating differential treatment of similarly situated non-speakers, even if not perfect one-to-one comparators at the pleading stage. This approach keeps the probable-cause rule intact in ordinary cases (Hartman v. Moore; Reichle v. Howards) while ensuring officials cannot weaponize rarely enforced offenses to punish protected speech.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett generally requires a § 1983 plaintiff bringing a retaliatory-arrest claim to plead and prove the absence of probable cause, but it also recognizes a narrow exception where objective evidence shows that similarly situated individuals not engaged in protected speech are typically not arrested. The Fifth Circuit’s near-identity comparator demand risks converting that exception into a nullity, inconsistent with Nieves’s text and its separation-of-powers-minded aim to use objective gates rather than subjective motive inquiries. Objective evidence may include more than one-to-one comparator arrests (e.g., enforcement patterns for a seldom-invoked statute and other non-motive indicia), so long as it plausibly shows differential treatment of similarly situated non-speakers, keeping the inquiry tethered to objective facts rather than intent. Remand is appropriate to apply that properly cabined standard without expanding damages liability beyond what Nieves allows.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Nieves v. Bartlett (2019), the existence of probable cause generally bars a § 1983 First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim, with only a narrow “objective evidence” exception designed to avoid intrusive motive inquiries and preserve administrable rules for officers and local governments. Consistent with Hartman v. Moore (2006) and Reichle v. Howards (2012), requiring a stringent, objective comparator-type showing (i.e., that similarly situated individuals not engaged in protected speech are typically not arrested for the same conduct) best aligns with history, workability, and judicial restraint by preventing probable cause from becoming merely “another part of the evidentiary mix.” While Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach (2018) recognizes that unusual retaliatory enforcement can be actionable, it does not displace Nieves’s probable-cause bar in ordinary arrest settings, and the Fifth Circuit’s demand for clear objective proof appropriately preserves the narrowness of the exception. Because Gonzalez had probable cause for arrest and has not shown the kind of objective non-arrest evidence Nieves contemplates, her claim should not proceed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Nieves v. Bartlett, the existence of probable cause generally defeats a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim, reflecting the causal and administrability concerns this Court emphasized in Hartman v. Moore and Reichle v. Howards. Nieves recognized a narrow exception where a plaintiff produces objective evidence that similarly situated individuals not engaged in protected speech were not arrested, but that carveout is best read as requiring concrete, comparative proof tied to ordinary enforcement practice rather than a more open-ended inquiry into contextual suspicion of animus. Expanding the exception to encompass non-comparator indicia would dilute the probable-cause rule into a motive-focused balancing test and invite broad discovery into subjective intent, contrary to Nieves’s methodological choice to use probable cause as an objective screen in § 1983 litigation. On this record as framed, the Fifth Circuit’s stringent approach better fits Nieves’s text and structure and preserves a workable line while leaving plaintiffs who can show differential enforcement to proceed.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett (2019) establishes a general probable-cause bar to First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claims, but it also recognizes an “objective evidence” exception where the plaintiff can show that similarly situated individuals not engaged in protected speech are typically not arrested for the same conduct—e.g., endemic or seldom-enforced offenses. Reading Nieves pragmatically and consistent with § 1983’s role in vindicating constitutional rights, that exception should not be collapsed into a near-identical-comparator demand at the pleading stage; objective indicia such as documented rarity of arrests under the statute, enforcement patterns, and other non-motive-based contextual facts can satisfy the threshold and permit the claim to proceed to ordinary causation proof. Hartman v. Moore (2006) and Reichle v. Howards (2012) reflect the Court’s concern about motive-heavy litigation, but Nieves itself calibrates that concern by allowing claims to proceed when objective evidence makes retaliation a plausible explanation despite probable cause. Therefore, where a plaintiff plausibly alleges objective evidence that the enforcement decision was aberrational compared to typical practice for similarly situated non-speakers, the claim should not be categorically barred simply because probable cause existed.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, in a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 where there was probable cause for the arrest, the plaintiff can satisfy the Nieves “similarly situated individuals not arrested” requirement by alleging objective circumstantial evidence of retaliation rather than identifying a near-identical comparator who was treated differently.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (retaliation for protected speech/petitioning) enforced via 42 U.S.C. § 1983; doctrine governing retaliatory arrest in light of probable cause (as articulated in Nieves v. Bartlett).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Gonzalez argues that the Fifth Circuit applied Nieves too rigidly by demanding she plead and prove a specific, nearly identical comparator who engaged in the same conduct but was not arrested. She contends Nieves created a narrow exception to the probable-cause bar that can be met through objective evidence showing retaliatory animus and atypical enforcement—especially where arrests for the charged conduct are rare and officials allegedly engineered the arrest after she criticized them (including by pursuing a criminal “tampering” theory over a trivial dispute and allegedly coordinating with police). In her view, requiring a perfect comparator is often impossible and would improperly insulate retaliatory arrests from First Amendment scrutiny even when the record strongly suggests retaliation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that because probable cause existed, Nieves generally bars a retaliatory-arrest claim and allows only a limited exception that requires objective proof in the form of a similarly situated non-arrestee comparator. They contend the Fifth Circuit correctly required Gonzalez to identify people who committed the same offense under similar circumstances but were not arrested; absent that showing, courts should not infer retaliation from motive allegations. Respondents (and supporting amici) emphasize administrability and separation-of-powers concerns: police and municipal officials make many discretionary enforcement choices, and loosening Nieves would invite pervasive litigation, discovery, and second-guessing of arrests supported by probable cause, potentially chilling legitimate law enforcement and local governance.
key_precedents: Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach (2018)
Mt. Healthy City School District Board of Education v. Doyle (1977)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that a rigid, nameable-comparator requirement could make Nieves’s qualification practically unavailable in low-level discretionary enforcement—has real force, and I agree with Justice Barrett that the evidence need not always be a single identified person. But Nieves’s carveout is written in explicitly comparative terms (“otherwise similarly situated individuals” committing the same conduct were not arrested), so any “objective evidence” must remain genuinely comparator-like (e.g., reliable, conduct-specific enforcement data or an established practice of non-arrest), not generalized circumstantial indicia that would predictably reintroduce motive-focused litigation and discovery burdens Nieves and Hartman sought to screen out when probable cause exists. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Lozman does not alter that conclusion because Lozman turned on a distinct municipal-policy record and our effort to keep that posture separate from on-the-scene arrest decisions; it is not a warrant to loosen Nieves into a free-form circumstantial test. On a minimalist, precedent-bound approach, I would affirm while making clear that the comparator need not be named, but the proof must be objective and conduct-specific in the way Nieves itself demands.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that a strict demand for a nameable, near-identical comparator may be impractical in low-level, discretionary policing, but that pragmatic concern cannot justify recasting Nieves’s narrow, comparative qualification into a “rarity/pattern” inquiry that predictably becomes a proxy for motive and defeats the probable-cause screen. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett correctly emphasize that Nieves’s text—“otherwise similarly situated individuals … not arrested”—requires an objective comparison tied to the same conduct; at most, that could include concrete enforcement data or a documented non-arrest practice, not generalized circumstantial indicia like escalation or animus. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Lozman does not alter my analysis because that case’s municipal-policy posture is exceptional and does not license expanding on-the-scene retaliatory-arrest claims where probable cause exists. Under a textualist and originalist approach, absent genuinely comparator-like proof of differential treatment for the same conduct, probable cause remains a bar to the § 1983 claim.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right to worry that requiring a single named “twin” comparator could make Nieves’s narrow qualification hard to invoke in some low-level discretionary contexts, but that policy concern cannot justify replacing Nieves’s comparative language with a free-form “objective circumstantial evidence” test that would predictably reopen motive-focused litigation whenever probable cause exists. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the qualification is written in conduct-specific comparative terms (“otherwise similarly situated individuals” engaged in the “same” conduct), and any permissible alternative to a named comparator must still function as a genuine benchmark of differential enforcement—e.g., concrete enforcement data or an established non-arrest practice—not generalized indicia like “rarity” untethered to similarly situated non-speakers. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Lozman does not alter my view because that case’s municipal-policy posture is exceptional and does not warrant diluting Nieves’s on-the-scene arrest framework into an amorphous inquiry. Under a textualist, administrability-focused reading, the Fifth Circuit may be too rigid in demanding an identified person, but petitioners’ broader approach is even less consistent with Nieves’s screening rule and institutional concerns.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s administrability concern is the hardest point for my side, and I accept their premise that Nieves must remain an objective, conduct-specific, genuinely comparative screen. But the Fifth Circuit’s rigidity—functionally demanding a nameable, near-identical comparator—misreads Nieves’s “otherwise similarly situated individuals” language and turns the “narrow qualification” into a dead letter precisely in the low-level discretionary arrests Nieves flagged as problematic; Justice Kagan is right that objective evidence can be comparative in substance through verifiable enforcement benchmarks (data, established non-arrest practice) without devolving into animus proof. Justice Alito’s worry that “objective circumstantial evidence” is amorphous is answered by cabining admissible proof to measurable, same-conduct differential enforcement rather than escalation narratives or generalized hostility, which keeps Hartman/Mt. Healthy causation workability intact. Lozman does not broaden the rule wholesale, but it supports the modest point that objective indicia beyond one-to-one comparators can be used when they remain concrete and verifiable; under a pragmatic approach attentive to access-to-justice realities, the respondent’s reading would immunize retaliation in exactly the settings where comparator identities are unknowable pre-discovery.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett make the strongest point on the other side: Nieves’s qualification must remain a genuinely comparative, conduct-specific, objective screen or else it collapses into the motive litigation Hartman/Nieves sought to avoid. But that administrability concern does not justify the Fifth Circuit’s rigidity, because “objective evidence” can still be comparator-like in substance—reliable enforcement data or an established non-arrest practice for the same conduct supplies the “otherwise similarly situated individuals” benchmark without requiring a named twin who is often unknowable in discretionary policing. Justice Thomas’s Whren-based worry is answered by insisting that the proof be verifiable and tied to differential enforcement for the charged conduct (not animus cues), preserving the objective screen while preventing the exception from becoming illusory. Lozman, as Roberts notes, is atypical, but it confirms that we can accept objective indicia beyond a one-to-one comparator when the evidence still operates comparatively and does not open the door to free-form motive inquiry.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point is administrability: the Nieves qualification must not become a motive-proxy that defeats the probable-cause screen. But their comparator-centric gloss cannot be read to require a named, near-identical comparator, because Nieves itself contemplated low-level discretionary enforcement where such a comparator will often be unknowable; “objective evidence” can instead be satisfied by verifiable, conduct-specific benchmarks (reliable enforcement data or an established non-arrest practice) that are genuinely comparative in substance. Justice Thomas’s Whren-based concern does not alter that analysis because Nieves already accepted a First Amendment retaliation claim notwithstanding probable cause and simply cabins it through an objective differential-treatment showing, not an inquiry into animus. Lozman, while factually distinctive as Roberts notes, reinforces that our doctrine can accept objective proof beyond a one-to-one comparator where it remains tightly tethered to causation and does not reopen subjective-motive litigation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that demanding a named, near-identical comparator can be unrealistic in low-level discretionary enforcement, and I agree with her (and Justice Barrett) that “objective evidence” need not be a single identifiable person and can include reliable enforcement data or an established non-arrest practice. But I do not think her proposed expansion can be untethered from Nieves’s comparative, conduct-specific framing—“otherwise similarly situated individuals” engaged in the “same” conduct—because that comparative anchor is what preserves the Hartman/Nieves administrability function and avoids reintroducing motive-driven discovery once probable cause exists, as the Chief Justice warns. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Lozman does not change the analysis for me: Lozman’s municipal-policy posture was expressly treated as exceptional, and using it to broaden Nieves for ordinary on-the-scene arrests risks collapsing the probable-cause screen into a generalized circumstantial inquiry. On a precedent-and-workability approach, the Fifth Circuit may have been too rigid if it demanded a named comparator in all cases, but the respondent still has the better reading so long as the standard is clarified to require genuinely comparator-like, conduct-specific objective proof rather than free-form indicia of animus.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point that a rigid demand for a named, near-identical comparator could render Nieves’s “narrow qualification” difficult to satisfy in low-level discretionary enforcement. But Nieves’s own text is comparative and conduct-specific—“otherwise similarly situated individuals” engaged in the “same” conduct—so “objective evidence” must still operate as a real comparator, whether via a named person, reliable enforcement data, or a demonstrated non-arrest practice for that same offense, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes. Expanding the qualification into a broader “rarity/pattern/escalation” circumstantial inquiry would predictably reintroduce motive-centered litigation and discovery burdens whenever probable cause exists, undermining the administrable screening rule Nieves adopted. Lozman, which Justice Sotomayor invokes, involved an alleged municipal policy in an atypical posture and does not justify loosening Nieves’s on-the-scene arrest framework beyond its conduct-specific comparative anchor.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern is the hardest point for petitioners, and I accept his premise that Nieves’s exception must remain comparative and conduct-specific to avoid routine motive discovery whenever probable cause exists. But Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s comparator framing does not require a rigid, nameable “near-identical” comparator as a threshold matter; consistent with Nieves’s own acknowledgment that an “unyielding” probable-cause bar can underprotect speech, “objective evidence” can be satisfied by verifiable enforcement benchmarks (documented non-arrest practice or reliable data) showing that arrests for the same conduct are atypical. Justice Thomas’s Whren analogy doesn’t move me because Fourth Amendment objective reasonableness does not resolve the First Amendment causation/screening problem addressed in Hartman, Mt. Healthy, and Nieves, and our task is to implement Nieves’s narrow qualification without making it illusory in precisely the low-level discretionary contexts it contemplated. Cabining the exception to genuinely comparative proof (not generalized animus) answers the Chief’s workability concern while preserving a meaningful remedy for retaliatory arrests.

John Roberts.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett held that the presence of probable cause generally defeats a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim, recognizing only a narrow exception where the plaintiff offers objective evidence that similarly situated individuals not engaged in the same protected speech were not arrested. Given that limiting principle, and the institutional and administrability concerns Nieves emphasized, we should not expand the exception to encompass generalized circumstantial proof untethered to comparative enforcement, which would risk converting the exception into the rule and invite routine litigation over arrests supported by probable cause. While Lozman involved a distinctive municipal policy context and did not displace Nieves’ probable-cause framework for ordinary arrests, Hartman’s causation concerns likewise support an objective, comparative showing to separate retaliatory motive from lawful enforcement. Respect for precedent and a narrow ruling counsel affirmance of the Fifth Circuit’s requirement that the exception be satisfied through comparator-type evidence rather than a free-ranging inquiry into motive whenever probable cause exists.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First Amendment contains no text authorizing courts to second-guess arrests supported by probable cause based on alleged retaliatory motive, and § 1983 supplies a cause of action only for actual constitutional violations, not freewheeling review of discretionary enforcement. In Nieves v. Bartlett (2019), this Court adopted a general probable-cause bar for retaliatory-arrest claims, recognizing only a narrow, administrable exception requiring objective evidence that similarly situated persons not engaged in protected speech were not arrested; that framework is consistent with Hartman v. Moore (2006)’s insistence on objective causation screens and with Whren v. United States (1996)’s refusal to make subjective intent dispositive where objective justification exists. Allowing “objective circumstantial evidence” untethered to a meaningful comparator would dilute Nieves’s limiting rule and invite motive-based litigation whenever probable cause exists, expanding federal judicial oversight beyond the Constitution’s original public meaning and proper separation of powers. Gonzalez therefore must satisfy Nieves through a genuine similarly situated non-arrestee comparison, not generalized circumstantial allegations.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett holds that the existence of probable cause generally defeats a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, with only a narrow, administrable exception requiring objective evidence that similarly situated individuals engaging in the same conduct were not arrested. Allowing plaintiffs to satisfy that requirement through amorphous “objective circumstantial evidence” of animus would effectively collapse Nieves into a motive inquiry, inviting broad discovery and second-guessing of routine enforcement decisions—precisely the practical consequences Nieves and Hartman v. Moore sought to avoid by using probable cause as a screening rule. The First Amendment does not authorize courts to invalidate arrests supported by probable cause based on speculative inferences about officials’ motives, and the comparator requirement provides the needed objective benchmark. This approach respects the textual limits of § 1983 and preserves law enforcement’s ability to enforce the criminal law without constant litigation over alleged retaliatory intent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett created a general probable-cause bar for § 1983 retaliatory-arrest damages claims but preserved a narrow pathway where the plaintiff supplies “objective evidence” that similarly situated individuals were not arrested; that language does not demand a near-identical, named comparator in every case, especially where enforcement is atypical and comparators are practically unknowable. Reading Nieves as the Fifth Circuit did would make probable cause an almost complete shield for retaliation against protected speech and petitioning, contrary to Nieves’s own concern that an “unyielding” rule would be “insufficiently protective of First Amendment rights,” and inconsistent with Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach’s recognition that objective circumstantial proof can establish retaliation. As in Mt. Healthy, the First Amendment requires a workable causation framework that does not immunize government officials from accountability when the record plausibly shows retaliatory motive plus unusual enforcement, particularly where the burdens fall on vulnerable speakers with limited access to evidence pre-discovery. Because § 1983 is a remedial statute meant to vindicate constitutional rights, the Nieves exception should be satisfied by objective circumstantial indicators of retaliation and selective enforcement, not only by a nearly perfect comparator.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett makes probable cause a general bar to retaliatory-arrest claims, but it also recognizes a “narrow qualification” where the plaintiff offers objective evidence that similarly situated people not engaged in the protected speech were not arrested; nothing in Nieves requires that objective evidence to take the rigid form of a near-identical named comparator. Reading the exception to demand a perfect match would make the carveout largely illusory in precisely the discretionary, low-level enforcement settings Nieves identified (and would depart from § 1983’s functional remedial role in policing First Amendment retaliation). Consistent with Nieves, Hartman v. Moore’s causation logic, and Lozman’s focus on objective indicia rather than motive alone, a plaintiff may satisfy the “similarly situated” requirement with objective circumstantial proof (e.g., arrest rarity data, established enforcement patterns, and unusual escalation) showing differential treatment tied to speech, while still keeping the rule workable and cabined. That approach preserves statutory coherence and administrability by requiring objective evidence of atypical enforcement, not merely allegations of animus, while avoiding an impossibly narrow comparator demand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett establishes a general probable-cause bar for retaliatory-arrest claims but preserves a “narrow qualification” when the plaintiff offers objective evidence that she was arrested while otherwise similarly situated individuals not engaged in the protected speech were not. Read according to its terms, that exception speaks to the kind of proof (objective evidence of atypical enforcement), not an inflexible pleading rule requiring a near-identical named comparator in every case; an atextual comparator-only requirement risks converting Nieves’s qualification into a nullity. Maintaining an objective-evidence inquiry also better fits separation-of-powers concerns identified in Nieves by avoiding freewheeling motive-based litigation while still allowing redress for retaliatory enforcement that departs from ordinary practice. This approach remains consistent with Hartman v. Moore’s causation-focused framework and avoids importing Whren v. United States’s Fourth Amendment objectivity principle to categorically foreclose First Amendment retaliation claims where enforcement is selectively weaponized.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett held that probable cause generally defeats a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim, recognizing only a narrow, administrable exception requiring objective evidence that “otherwise similarly situated individuals” not engaged in the plaintiff’s protected speech were not arrested. Expanding that exception to include broad “objective circumstantial evidence” untethered to a meaningful comparator would undermine Nieves’s core workability rationale and invite motive-based litigation and discovery whenever probable cause exists, contrary to Hartman v. Moore’s causation concerns and the Court’s traditional reluctance to constitutionalize discretionary enforcement judgments. While Lozman shows the Court can allow a tailored path in unusual, institutionally sensitive settings, it did so on a very specific record and did not displace Nieves’s general probable-cause rule. Respecting precedent and maintaining clear, workable lines counsels adhering to Nieves’s comparator-focused framework rather than converting it into a generalized circumstantial-evidence inquiry.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett held that when probable cause supports an arrest, a First Amendment retaliatory-arrest claim is generally barred, with only a “narrow qualification” requiring “objective evidence” that “otherwise similarly situated individuals” engaged in the “same” conduct but were not arrested. 139 S. Ct. 1715, 1727 (2019). That language is comparative and conduct-specific; reading it to allow non-comparator circumstantial proof would dilute Nieves’s administrable line and collapse the probable-cause rule into a motive inquiry, contrary to the Court’s concern (echoing Hartman v. Moore) about inferring retaliation where lawful enforcement grounds exist. Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach does not compel a broader exception because it addressed a distinct context involving an alleged official municipal policy of retaliation, not the standard on-the-scene arrest case governed by Nieves. Given the textual specificity of Nieves’s exception and the need for methodological consistency in First Amendment retaliation doctrine under § 1983, the Fifth Circuit’s comparator-focused approach best fits the governing precedent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Nieves v. Bartlett (2019) makes probable cause generally dispositive in retaliatory-arrest claims, but its “narrow exception” turns on whether arrests for the charged conduct are typically not made and requires “objective evidence” that retaliation drove this arrest; that objective showing should not be rigidly confined to a near-identical, nameable comparator when other circumstantial, verifiable proof can demonstrate atypical enforcement. Reading Nieves to demand a practically unattainable comparator in many contexts would undermine procedural fairness and insulate purposeful retaliation against protected First Amendment petitioning and speech enforced via 42 U.S.C. § 1983, contrary to the core principle that government may not punish criticism. This approach is consistent with Lozman v. City of Riviera Beach (2018), which permitted a retaliatory-arrest claim to proceed despite probable cause where the record contained objective evidence of an official plan to retaliate, and it respects Mt. Healthy’s causation framework by still requiring proof that protected activity was the but-for cause. Limiting “objective evidence” to only comparator evidence would elevate administrability over constitutional accountability and would invite arbitrary disparities—especially in discretionary, low-level enforcement—without a meaningful First Amendment remedy.
